Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verses 1–3:

Surat al-Ahqaf is Meccan, according to all of them. It has thirty-four verses, though it is said to have five.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿Ha, Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth and for a specified term. But those who disbelieve turn away from what they are warned of.﴾

Regarding His saying, the Exalted: "Ha, Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise." This has already been discussed [[See p. 156 of this part.]]. "We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth" has also already been discussed [[See vol. 10, p. 53.]]. "And for a specified term" means the Resurrection, according to the view of Ibn 'Abbas and others. It is the term at which the heavens and the earth come to an end. It is also said that it refers to the term decreed for every created being. "But those who disbelieve turn away from what they are warned of" — they were warned, frightened — "turn away" means turn their backs, heedless, unprepared for it. It is also permissible that "ma" (what) be a verbal-masdar (ma masdariyya), meaning: "turn away from their being warned of that Day."

**Issue one:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: Have you considered what you invoke besides Allah?﴾ That is, what you worship of idols and rivals besides Allah. "Show me what they have created of the earth," that is, have they created anything of the earth? "Or have they a share" (*shirk*), that is, a portion, "in the heavens," that is, in the creation of the heavens alongside Allah. "Bring me a Book before this," that is, before this Qur'an.

**Issue two:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿or a remnant of knowledge﴾. The common reading is "aw athāratin" with an alif after the thā'. Ibn 'Abbās said, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is the line that the Arabs used to draw in the earth." This was mentioned by al-Mahdawī and al-Tha'labī. Ibn al-'Arabī said: "It is not authentically established." A well-known hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) says: "A prophet among the prophets used to draw lines; whoever's line agrees with his, that is it." This is also not authentically established. I say: it is established from the hadith of Mu'āwiyah ibn al-Ḥakam al-Sulamī, which Muslim narrated. Al-Naḥḥās related with a chain: "Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad (known as al-Jarāyijī)" — the manuscripts vary in writing this nisba — said: Muḥammad ibn Bundār told us, who said: Yaḥyā ibn Sa'īd told us, from Sufyān al-Thawrī, from Ṣafwān ibn Sulaym, from Abū Salamah, from Ibn 'Abbās, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding his saying, mighty and majestic is He, "or a remnant of knowledge," that he said: "It is the line." This is also authentic.

Ibn al-'Arabī said: The scholars differed in its interpretation. Some said it came to permit line-drawing, because some of the prophets did it. Others said it came to forbid it, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever's line agrees with his, that is it," and there is no way to know the method of the earlier prophet in it, so there is no way to act upon it. He said:

*By your life, the strikers with pebbles do not know,*
*nor do the bird-augurs, what Allah is doing.*
(The verse is by Labīd. The reading in it is "al-ṭawāriq" instead of "al-ḍawārib." *Al-ṭarq* is striking with pebbles. *Al-ṭawāriq* are those who foretell by the stars.)

Its reality, according to its practitioners, returns to the forms of the stars. What emerges from them indicates what those stars indicate of good fortune or misfortune that will befall people. Thus it became conjecture built upon conjecture, and attachment to a hidden matter whose path has been obliterated and whose verification has been lost. The Sharī'ah (sacred law) has forbidden it and informed that this is among what Allah has singled out for Himself and cut off from creation. Even if they had, before that, means by which they grasped hidden things, Allah has removed those means, erased those doors, and reserved knowledge of the unseen for Himself. It is not permissible to contest Him in this, and it is not lawful for anyone to claim it. Seeking it would be futile even without a prohibition; but since a prohibition has come, seeking it is disobedience or disbelief, according to the intention of the seeker.

I say: what he chose is the view of al-Khaṭṭābī. Al-Khaṭṭābī said: His saying, peace be upon him: [(*ma bayna al-murabba'ayn* is omitted in ka and h.)] "Whoever's line agrees with his, that is it" — this may imply a prohibition, since that was a sign of his prophethood and it has ended, so we have been forbidden to engage in it. Qāḍī 'Iyāḍ said: The more apparent meaning of the wording is the opposite of this, namely the approval of the line of whoever agrees with his line. But how can agreement be known when the Sharī'ah forbids conjecture and claiming the unseen altogether? Its meaning is that whoever's line agrees with his is the one whose accuracy they find, not that he intends to permit this practice to its practitioner as some of them interpreted it. Makkī related, in his commentary on the saying "a prophet among the prophets used to draw lines," that he used to draw with his index and middle fingers in the sand and then divine. [(The clause "that he used to draw" is omitted in l and z.)] Ibn 'Abbās said, in explaining the verse ﴿and among us are men who draw lines﴾: it is the line drawn by the *ḥāzī* (diviner).

He is given a gift, and he says: "Sit until I draw for you." In front of the diviner is a boy holding a stick. Then he comes to soft ground, and the master draws lines rapidly so that they cannot be counted. Then he returns and erases them slowly, two by two. If two lines remain, it is a sign of success; if one line remains, it is a sign of failure. The Arabs call it *al-asḥam*, and it is considered ominous among them.

**Issue three:** Ibn al-'Arabī said: Allah the Exalted has left no means indicating the unseen, which He permitted one to rely upon and derive inference from, except dreams. He permitted them and informed that they are a part of prophethood. Likewise *al-fa'l* (good omen). As for *al-ṭiyarah* (bad omen) and *al-zajr* (augury), He forbade both. *Al-fa'l* is inferring from what one hears of speech regarding what one intends of a matter, when it is good. If he hears something disagreeable, it is *ṭiyarah*. The Sharī'ah commanded him to rejoice at the good omen and proceed with his affair gladly. When he hears something disliked, he turns away from it and does not return on account of it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, there is no omen but Your omen, no good but Your good, and no god other than You." Some men of letters have related:

*Good omen, augury, and soothsayers are all*
*misleading, and behind the unseen are locks.*

This is sound speech, except regarding good omen, for the Sharī'ah excepted it and commanded it. So what this poet composed about it is not accepted, for he spoke in ignorance, and the Lawgiver is more truthful, more knowing, and more wise.

I say: What has passed concerning *al-ṭiyarah* and *al-fa'l*, and the distinction between them, in (*al-Mā'idah*) [(See vol. 6, p. 59 onward.)] and elsewhere, is sufficient. And it passed in (*al-An'ām*) [(See vol. 7, p. 2.)] that Allah, glorified is He, is alone in knowledge of the unseen, and that no one knows it except what Allah makes known to him, or what He places as a customary indication by which what happens according to the ordinary course can be known, and this may vary. An example: when one sees a palm tree that has put forth its spathe, he knows it will bear fruit; and when he sees its pollen scattered, he knows it will not bear fruit. Yet it is possible that a blight may come upon it and destroy its fruit so it does not bear, just as it is possible that the palm whose pollen was scattered may have Allah bring forth a second spathe in it, and it bears fruit. And just as it is also possible that no month follows its month and no day follows its day, if Allah wills to annihilate the world at that time. Other matters are explained in (*al-An'ām*) as previously stated.

**Issue four:** Ibn Khuwayz Mandād said: The saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿or a remnant of knowledge﴾, means the line. Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, used to judge by handwriting when a witness recognized his handwriting, and when a judge recognized his handwriting or the handwriting of the one who wrote to him, he would rule accordingly. Then he retracted this when the deceptions and forgeries that appeared among the people became apparent. It is related from him that he said: "People will commit wickedness, and so judgments will arise for them." But when witnesses testify to a handwriting that is the subject of the ruling, such as testifying that this is the handwriting and document of the judge, the judge may consider them to have made him witness to what is in it, even if they do not know what is in the document. Likewise a bequest, or a man's handwriting acknowledging money owed to another, which witnesses testify is his handwriting, and the like. The school's position on this does not differ: he rules by it.

It is said that "or a remnant of knowledge" means "or a remainder of knowledge," as said by Ibn 'Abbās, al-Kalbī, Abū Bakr ibn 'Ayyāsh, and others. In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* (the lexicon): "*aw athāratin min 'ilmin*" means a remainder of it. Likewise *al-athārah* (with a vowel on the letters) is the same. It is said: the camels grew fat "on *athārah*," meaning a remainder of fat that existed before that. Al-Māwardī and al-Tha'labī recited the verse of al-Rā'ī:

*And a she-camel of remainder, eating upon it*
*plants in its heights, and so she leaped away.*

Al-Harawī said: *al-athārah* and *al-athar* mean a remainder. It is said: "There is no trace or remnant there." Maymūn ibn Mihrān, Abū Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Raḥmān, and Qatādah said: "or a remnant of knowledge" means a special portion of knowledge. Mujāhid said: a transmission you transmit from those who came before you. 'Ikrimah and Muqātil said: a narration from the prophets. Al-Qurazī said: it is the *isnād* (chain of transmission). Al-Ḥasan said: the meaning is something that is stirred up or extracted. Al-Zajjāj said: "*aw athāratin*" means a sign. *Al-athārah* is a verbal noun like *al-samāḥah* and *al-shajā'ah*. The root of the word is from *al-athar*, which is transmission. It is said: "I transmitted the hadith, I transmit it, *athran* and *athārah* and *uthrah*, so I am one who transmits (*āthir*), when you mention it from someone else." From this it is said: a hadith is *ma'thūr* (transmitted), meaning one successor has taken it from a predecessor. Al-A'shā said:

*Indeed, that which you two disputed about*
*has been made clear to the hearer and the transmitter.*

It is narrated "bayn" (between), and it is recited "*aw uthratin*" with a damma on the hamza and sukūn on the thā'. It may be that its meaning is a remainder of knowledge. It may be that its meaning is something transmitted from the books of the ancients. *Al-ma'thūr* is what is spoken of that has a sound chain back to the one from whom it is narrated. [(The word "'anhu" is omitted in z and l.)] Al-Sulamī, al-Ḥasan, and Abū Rajā' recited with a fatḥah on the hamza and the thā' without an alif, meaning a special portion of knowledge given to you or preferred for you over others. It is also narrated from al-Ḥasan and a group "*athratin*" with a fatḥah on the alif and sukūn on the thā'. Al-Tha'labī mentioned the first, and al-Māwardī the second. Al-Tha'labī related from 'Ikrimah: "*aw mīrāthin min 'ilmin*" (or an inheritance of knowledge). ﴿If you are truthful.﴾

**Issue five:** The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Bring me a Book before this or a remnant of knowledge﴾ contains an explanation of all the paths of evidence. The first of them is reason, which is His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered what you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created of the earth, or have they a share in the heavens?﴾ This is an argument by the evidence of reason that an inanimate object cannot validly be called upon besides Allah, for it neither harms nor benefits. Then He said: ﴿Bring me a Book before this﴾, which contains the evidence of revelation (*al-samʿ*), ﴿or a remnant of knowledge﴾.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And who is more astray﴾, meaning: there is no one more astray and more ignorant "than one who calls upon other than Allah those who will not answer him until the Day of Resurrection," and they are the idols. "And they are heedless of their calling" meaning: they do not hear and do not understand. So He spoke of them, though they are inanimate objects, in the manner of male human beings, since their worshippers had likened them to kings and rulers who are served.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verse 6:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when mankind are gathered﴾, meaning on the Day of Resurrection. "They will be enemies to them" — that is, these objects of worship will be enemies to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection. So the angels are enemies of the disbelievers, and the jinn and the devils will disown their worshippers tomorrow, and some of them will curse one another. It is also possible that the idols will be enemies to the disbelievers who worshipped them, on the assumption that life is created in them. The evidence for this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿We disown You; they never used to worship us﴾ [[Qur'an 28:63.]] [Al-Qasas: 63]. It has also been said: they will turn against their objects of worship, because these were the cause of their destruction, and the objects of worship will deny their worship, and this is His saying: "and they will be disbelievers in their worship."
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them as clear proofs﴾ — meaning the Qur'an. "Those who disbelieve say of the truth when it comes to them, 'This is clear magic.'"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ The mim is a connecting particle (silah). The sense is: "Do they say, 'He invented it'?" That is, "Muhammad fabricated it (taqawwalahu)." This is a shift (idrab) away from mentioning their naming of the signs as sorcery. The meaning of the hamza in "am" (or) is denunciation (inkar) and wonder (ta'ajjub), as if He said: "Leave this aside, and listen to their statement, which is reprehensible and deserving of wonder." That is because Muhammad was not able to produce it unless he uttered it and fabricated it against Allah. And if he had been able to produce it while the Arab nation was not, his ability to do so would have been a miracle (mu'jizah), since it breaks the customary course; and if it were a miracle, it would be a confirmation from Allah of him. The Wise does not confirm a liar, so he would not be a fabricator. The pronoun refers to the truth (al-haqq), and what is meant by it is the signs (al-ayat). ﴿Say: "If I have invented it"﴾ by way of supposition (ʿala sabil al-fard). ﴿then you cannot avail me anything against Allah﴾ meaning you cannot ward off the punishment of Allah from me, so how would I fabricate against Allah for your sake. ﴿He knows best what you are busy with therein﴾ meaning what you say, according to Mujahid. It was also said: what you plunge into of denial. The ifada in a thing is plunging into it and rushing forward in it. They "afadu fi al-hadith" meaning they rushed into it. And "afada al-ba'ir" meaning he expelled his cud from his paunch and brought it out, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"And they poured forth after their being held back, with a belch [[This is the second half of a verse by al-Ra'i, whose first half, as in Yaqut's Mu'jam al-Buldan under "Huqayl", is:

From Dhu al-Abariq when they grazed Huqayl.

Dhu al-Abariq and Huqayl are one place. He says: they were holding back from thirst (al-kazum among camels is the one who withholds the cud), so when what was in their bellies became wet, they poured forth a belch.]] And "afada al-nas min Arafat ila Mina," meaning they were pushed, and every push is an ifada. ﴿Sufficient is He as a witness﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). ﴿between me and you﴾ meaning He knows my truthfulness and that you are the falsifiers. ﴿And He is the Forgiving﴾ to whoever repents, ﴿the Merciful﴾ toward His believing servants.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verse 9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say, I am not a novelty among the messengers﴾, i.e., I am not the first to be sent; messengers came before me, related from Ibn 'Abbas and others. Al-bid' (novelty) means "the first." 'Ikrimah and others read "bidaʻan" with a fatha on the dal, on the assumption that a noun has been omitted, and the meaning is: "I am not a possessor of novelty." It has also been said that bid' and badi' have the same meaning, like nisf and nasif. Abda'a al-sha'ir means he came with something original (al-badi'). Shay' bid' (with a kasra) means mubtada' (something newly invented). Fulan bid' fi hadha al-amr means he is unique (badi') in this matter. Qawm abda' (a people) is reported from al-Akhfash. Qutrub recited the verse of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

"So I am not a novelty among the events that befall men, who after misery became happy."

[[This is the wording of the verse as it appears in the manuscripts of the original. In the Christian poets' collection, however, it reads: "So you are not one who fears the events that befall men, so they hastened after misery to happiness."]]

﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾, meaning on the Day of Resurrection. When this was revealed, the polytheists, the Jews and the hypocrites rejoiced and said: "How can we follow a prophet who does not know what will be done with him or with us, and who has no superiority over us? If he had not invented what he says on his own initiative, the One who sent him would have told him what will be done with him." Then it was revealed: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your sins, past and future﴾ [al-Fath: 2], which abrogated this verse, and Allah humbled the noses of the disbelievers. The Companions said: "Congratulations to you, O Messenger of Allah! Allah has made clear to you what will be done with you, O Messenger of Allah; so what will He do with us?" Then it was revealed: ﴿That He may admit the believing men and believing women into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ [al-Fath: 5], and so on. And it was revealed: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that they will have from Allah a great bounty﴾ [al-Ahzab: 47]. This was said by Anas, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak.

Umm al-'Ala', a woman of the Ansar, said: "We drew lots for the Muhajirun, and 'Uthman ibn Maz'un ibn Huzafah ibn Jumah fell to us. We lodged him in our houses, and he died. I said: 'May Allah's mercy be upon you, Abu al-Sa'ib! Indeed Allah has honoured you.' The Prophet ﷺ said: [And what makes you know that Allah has honoured him?] I said: 'May my father and mother be ransomed for you, O Messenger of Allah! Then who?' He said: [As for him, certainty has come to him, and we have seen nothing but good for him. By Allah, I hope for Paradise for him. By Allah, I am the Messenger of Allah, and I do not know what will be done with me or with you.] She said: 'By Allah, I will never again declare anyone pure after him.' al-Tha'labi mentioned it and said: He said this when he did not yet know that his sins had been forgiven, for Allah forgave him his sin at the expedition of al-Hudaybiyah, four years before his death.

I say: The hadith of Umm al-'Ala' was narrated by al-Bukhari, and my narration of it reads: "And I do not know what will be done with him," which does not contain "with me or with you." This is the sound version, Allah willing, as will be explained.

The verse is not abrogated, because it is a statement of information. al-Nahhas said: It is impossible that there be an abrogating or abrogated element in this from two aspects. One is that it is a statement of information. The other is that from the beginning of the surah up to this point, it is addressed to the polytheists, argues against them and rebukes them, so this too must be addressed to the polytheists, as was the case before and after it. And it is impossible that the Prophet ﷺ would say to the polytheists, "I do not know what will be done with me or with you" in the Hereafter, when from the beginning of his mission until his death he ﷺ never ceased to inform that whoever dies in disbelief is eternal in the Fire, and whoever dies in faith and follows and obeys him is in Paradise. He ﷺ had therefore seen what would be done with him and with them in the Hereafter. It is not permissible that he say to them, "I do not know what will be done with me or with you in the Hereafter," for they would then say, "How can we follow you when you do not know whether you will go to ease and tranquillity or to punishment and retribution?"

The correct view regarding the verse is the saying of al-Hasan, as Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn Hafs recited from Yusuf ibn Musa, who said: Waki' narrated to us, who said: Abu Bakr al-Hudhali narrated to us, from al-Hasan: "And I do not know what will be done with me or with you in the world." Abu Ja'far said: This is the most sound and the best of the opinions: he ﷺ did not know what would befall him and them of illness and health, cheapness and dearness, wealth and poverty. Similar to it is: ﴿Had I known the unseen, I would have acquired much good, and no evil would have touched me; I am only a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾ [al-A'raf: 188].

al-Wahidi and others mentioned, from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas: When the affliction intensified upon the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he saw in a dream that he would migrate to a land of palm trees, trees and water. He related it to his Companions, and they rejoiced at this and saw in it relief from what they were suffering of the harm of the polytheists. Then they remained for a while without seeing it, and they said: "O Messenger of Allah, when shall we migrate to the land you saw?" The Prophet ﷺ fell silent, and Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾, meaning: I do not know whether I will go out to the place I saw in my dream or not. Then he said: [It is only something I saw in my dream. I follow only what is revealed to me], meaning: what I have told you has not been revealed to me.

al-Qushayri said: According to this, there is no abrogation in the verse. It has also been said: the meaning is, "I do not know what will be prescribed upon me and upon you of obligations." al-Tabari chose that the meaning is: I do not know what my affair and your affair will come to in the world: whether you will believe or disbelieve, whether you will be hastened with punishment or be delayed.

I say: This is the meaning of the saying of al-Hasan, al-Suddi and others. al-Hasan said: "I do not know what will be done with me or with you" in the world; as for the Hereafter, God forbid! He knew that he was in Paradise when He took his covenant from the messengers. Rather, he said: "I do not know what will be done with me in the world: will I be driven out as the prophets before me were driven out, or will I be killed as the prophets before me were killed? And I do not know what will be done with you: will your nation be the believing one or the denying one, or my nation that is pelted with stones from heaven, or swallowed up by the earth?" Then there was revealed: ﴿He it is who sent His messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, that He may make it prevail over all religion﴾ [al-Tawbah: 33], meaning: He will make His religion prevail over the religions. Then He said concerning his nation: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33]. Thus Allah informed him of what He would do with him and with his nation, and there is no abrogation in all of this, and praise be to Allah.

al-Dahhak also said: "I do not know what will be done with me or with you" means: what you will be commanded and forbidden. It has also been said: the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to say to the believers, "I do not know what will be done with me or with you on the Day of Resurrection," then Allah the Exalted clarified that in His saying: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your sins, past and future﴾ [al-Fath: 2], and then clarified after that the state of the believers, then the state of the disbelievers.

I say: This is the meaning of the first opinion, except that "abrogation" was used in it in the sense of "clarification," and that he was commanded to say that to the believers. The sound view is what we have mentioned from al-Hasan and others.

The "ma" in "ma yuf'alu" may be relative (mawsulah), or it may be interrogative in the nominative case. ﴿I follow only what is revealed to me, and I am only a clear warner﴾. It is read "yuhá" (yūḥā), i.e., by Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This has been discussed previously in other places.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is from Allah﴾, means the Qur'an. "And you disbelieve in it." Al-Sha'bi said: the intended one is Muhammad (ﷺ). "And a witness from the Children of Israel testified" ﴿and a witness from the Children of Israel testified﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and Mujahid said: he is 'Abdullah ibn Salam, who testified against the Jews that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is mentioned in the Torah, and that he is a prophet from Allah. In al-Tirmidhi, from him: "Verses of the Book of Allah were revealed concerning me: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to the like of it, and believed, but you were arrogant. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾" This has already been mentioned at the end of surah al-Ra'd [[see vol. 9, p. 335]]. Masruq said: he is Musa and the Torah, not Ibn Salam, because he embraced Islam in Medina, and the surah is Meccan (makkiyyah). He also said: "And you disbelieve in it" is addressed to the Quraysh. Al-Sha'bi said: he is one of the Children of Israel who believed in Musa and the Torah, because Ibn Salam only embraced Islam two years before the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the surah is Meccan. Al-Qushayri said: whoever says the witness is Musa also says the surah is Meccan, and Ibn Salam embraced Islam two years before the death of the Prophet (ﷺ) [[what is between the two brackets is missing from manuscript K.]]. It is possible that the verse was revealed in Medina and placed in a Meccan surah, since a verse would be revealed and the Prophet (ﷺ) would say: "Place it in the surah of such-and-such." The verse is in the context of disputing with the polytheists, and the argument's basis is that they used to refer to the Jews regarding matters; that is, their testimony for them and the testimony of their Prophet for me is among the clearest proofs. It is not unlikely that the surah is in the context of disputing with the Jews. When Ibn Salam came as a Muslim before the Jews knew of his embracing Islam, he said: "O Messenger of Allah, make me an arbiter between you and the Jews." So he (ﷺ) asked them about him: "What sort of man is he among you?" They said: "Our chief and our scholar." He said: "Indeed he has believed in me." Then they spoke ill of him... the hadith.

This has already been mentioned. Ibn 'Abbas said: the Jews accepted the judgment of Ibn Salam, and they said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If he testifies for you, we will believe in you." So he was asked and he testified, then he embraced Islam. "Upon the like of it," that is, upon the like of what I have brought to you: Musa testified to the Torah, and Muhammad testified to the Qur'an. Al-Jurjani said: "mithl" (مِثْلِ, "like") is a ṣilah (a filler or connecting element, grammatically superfluous), meaning: and a witness from among them testified to it, that it is from Allah. "Then he believed," that is, this witness. "But you were arrogant," you yourselves, toward belief. The answer to "in kana" (إِنْ كانَ, "if it be") is omitted, and its estimate is: "Then he believed; will you believe?" This was said by al-Zajjaj. It was also said: "Then he believed, and you were arrogant, are you not then wrongdoers?" which is clarified by "Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people." It was also said: "Then he believed, and you were arrogant; will you then be secure from the punishment of Allah?" "Ara'aytum" (أَرَأَيْتُمْ, "have you considered") is a word established for asking and interrogation, and for that reason it does not require an object. Al-Naqqash and others related that there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the verse, and its estimate is: "Say: Have you considered, if it is from Allah, and a witness from the Children of Israel testified, then he believed, while you disbelieved? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it."﴾ Scholars differed regarding the occasion of its revelation, into six [[So it stands in the copies of the original. It is noted that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned five opinions.]] opinions:

The first: that Abu Dharr al-Ghifari was invited to Islam by the Prophet (ﷺ) in Makkah and responded. His people sought his protection, so their chief came to him and embraced Islam, then the chief invited them and they embraced Islam. This reached Quraysh, and they said: "Ghifar, the allies, had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it." So this verse was revealed. This was related by Abu al-Mutawakkil.

The second: that Zunayrah [[Zunayrah (with a kasra on the zay and a shadda on the kasra-marked nun): a Roman woman. She was among the earliest to embrace Islam and among those tortured for the sake of Allah. Abu Jahl used to torture her. She is one of the seven whom Abu Bakr al-Siddiq bought and freed from torture.]] embraced Islam and her sight was afflicted, so they said to her: "Al-Lat and al-Uzza have struck you," but Allah restored her sight. The chiefs of Quraysh then said: "Had what Muhammad brought been good, Zunayrah would not have preceded us to it." So Allah revealed this verse. This was related by Urwah ibn al-Zubayr.

The third: that those who disbelieved were the Banu Amir, Ghatafan, Tamim, Asad, Hanzalah and Ashja', who said to those from Ghifar who had embraced Islam, and Juhaynah, Muzaynah and Khuza'ah: "Had what Muhammad brought been good, the shepherds of the goats would not have preceded us to it, since we are more honored than them." This was said by al-Kalbi and al-Zajjaj, and al-Qushayri related it from Ibn Abbas. Qatadah said: it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Quraysh, who said: "Had what Muhammad calls us to been good, Bilal, Suhayb, Ammar, so-and-so and so-and-so would not have preceded us to it." This is the fourth opinion.

The fifth: that those who disbelieved among the Jews said to those who believed, meaning Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions: "Had the religion of Muhammad been true, they would not have preceded us to it." This was said by most of the exegetes, related by al-Tha'labi. Masruq said: the disbelievers said, "Had it been good, the Jews would not have preceded us to it," so this verse was revealed.

This objection from the disbelievers in their saying, "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it," is among the greatest objections, since it turns back upon them against anyone who opposes them, so that it may be said to them: "Had what you are upon been good, we would not have turned away from it; had your denial of the Messenger been good, you would not have preceded us to it." This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Then it has been said: the phrase "they would not have preceded us to it" may be the speech of the disbelievers to some of the believers, and it may be a shift from address to third person, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿until when you are in the ship and they sail with them﴾ [[Verse 22 of Surah Yunus.]] [Yunus: 22]. "And since they have not been guided by it" means the faith. It has also been said: the Qur'an. It has also been said: Muhammad (ﷺ). "Then they will say, 'This is an ancient falsehood'" means: since they did not attain guidance through the Qur'an nor through the one who brought it, they opposed him, attributed him to lying, and said, "This is an ancient falsehood," just as they said, "Legends of the ancients." It was said to someone: "Is there in the Qur'an that whoever is ignorant of something opposes it?" He said: "Yes." Allah the Exalted says: "And since they have not been guided by it, they will say, 'This is an ancient falsehood.'" And similar to it is ﴿Rather, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge﴾ [[Verse 39 of Surah Yunus.]] [Yunus: 39].

**"And before it"**, that is, before the Qur'an, **"the Book of Moses"**, that is, the Torah, **"as a guide"**, to be followed in what it contains, **"and a mercy"** from God. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "but you did not take guidance from it." This is because the Torah contained a description of the Prophet ﷺ and a command to believe in him, and they abandoned that.

**"As a guide"** (*imaman*) is in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial accusative), because the meaning is: "and the Book of Moses went before it as a guide." **"And a mercy"** is coordinated with it (*ma'tuf 'alayh*). It was also said that it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: "We sent it down as a guide and a mercy." Al-Akhfash said it is in the accusative as a *qat'* (a detached, non-restrictive accusative), because "the Book of Moses" is definite by virtue of the *idafa* (construct phrase). When an indefinite noun is repeated, or made into a construct, or given the definite article, it becomes definite.

**"And this is a Book"**, meaning the Qur'an, **"confirming"**, meaning confirming the Torah and the other books before it. It was also said: confirming the Prophet ﷺ.

**"In an Arabic tongue"** is in the accusative as a *hal*, meaning: confirming what came before it, being in Arabic. **"Tongue"** (*lisanan*) is a *tawti'a* (preparatory accusative) for the *hal*, that is, an emphasis, like the saying: "Zayd came to me a righteous man," where you mention "a man" as emphasis. It was also said that it is in the accusative by an implied verb, its estimate being: "and this is a Book confirming; I mean an Arabic tongue." It was also said that it is in the accusative by dropping the preposition, its estimate being: "in an Arabic tongue." It was also said that *lisan* is the object, and that what is meant by it is the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: "and this is a Book confirming the Prophet ﷺ, because it is his miracle," and the estimate is: "confirming one who has an Arabic tongue." So *lisan* is in the accusative by *musaddiq* (confirming), and it refers to the Prophet ﷺ. It is unlikely that *lisan* means the Qur'an, because the meaning would then be that it confirms itself.

**"To warn those who have wronged"**: the reading of the common majority is *li-yundhira* with the *ya'* (third person), as a predicate about the Book, meaning: "that it may warn those who have wronged themselves through disbelief and disobedience." It was also said that it is a predicate about the Messenger ﷺ. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Bazzi read it with the *ta'* (second person), addressing the Prophet ﷺ, and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading. God says: ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]. [[See vol. 9, p. 285.]]

**"And good tidings to the doers of good"**: *bushra* is in the nominative position, meaning: "and it is good tidings." It was also said that it is coordinated with "the Book," meaning: "this is a confirming Book and good tidings." It is also permissible that it is in the accusative by dropping the preposition, meaning: "that it may warn those who have wronged, and for good tidings," and when the preposition was dropped, it became accusative. It was also said that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: "and it gives good tidings to the doers of good with good tidings," and when it is put in place of "and gives good tidings," as "good tidings" or "a glad tiding," it becomes accusative, just as you say: "I came to you to visit you, and as an honour to you and a fulfilment of your right," meaning: "to visit you, and to honour you, and to fulfil your right," so the word "honour" is accusative by a hidden verb.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on verses 13–14 of surah 46:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast﴾ and the rest of the verse. Its meaning has already been discussed [[See vol. 15, p. 357]]. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. The verse is general in its application. The word "جزاء" (jaza', "recompense") is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar, a noun derived from the verb that expresses the action itself).

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on verses 13–14 of surah 46:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast﴾ and the rest of the verse. Its meaning has already been discussed [[See vol. 15, p. 357]]. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. The verse is general in its application. The word "جزاء" (jaza', "recompense") is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar, a noun derived from the verb that expresses the action itself).

**First issue:** He says: "And We have enjoined upon man goodness to his parents" ﴿And We have enjoined upon man (to be good) to his parents﴾. It explains the difference in a person's condition toward his parents: sometimes he obeys them and sometimes he opposes them. That is, a similar situation is not far-fetched in the case of the Prophet ﷺ and his people, so that some respond to him and some disbelieve. This is the connection between the parts of the discourse, as al-Qushayri said.

**Second issue:** His saying, "ḥasanan" (goodness). The common reading is "ḥusnan," and it is so in the codices of the people of the two Sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah), Basra and Syria. Ibn ʿAbbas and the Kufans read "iḥsanan," and their evidence is His saying in Surat al-Anʿam and Banu Israʾil: ﴿and to the parents, goodness﴾ [al-Anʿam: 151] [Verse 151, Surah al-Anʿam; verse 23, Surah al-Isra']. It is also so in the codices of Kufa. The evidence for the first reading is His saying in Surat al-ʿAnkabut: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man (goodness) to his parents﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 8] [Verse 8], and they did not differ about it. *Al-ḥusn* is the opposite of ugliness (*qubḥ*), and *al-iḥsan* is the opposite of wrongdoing (*isa'a*). *Al-tawṣiya* means command. The discussion of this and of whom it was revealed about has already passed [see vol. 13, p. 328].

**Third issue:** His saying: ﴿His mother bore him with hardship, and gave birth to him with hardship﴾. That is, with difficulty and hardship. The common reading is with a *fatḥa* on the *kāf* (*karhan*). Abu ʿUbayd chose this and said: "Likewise the word *al-karh* throughout the Quran is with a *fatḥa*, except in Surat al-Baqara: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqara: 216], because that is a noun (*ism*), whereas these are all verbal nouns (*maṣādir*)." The Kufans read *kurhan* with a *ḍamma*. It is said that they are two dialects, like *al-ḍuʿf* and *al-ḍaʿf*, and *al-shuhd* and *al-shahd*. This was said by al-Kisa'i, and it is likewise the view of all the Basran grammarians. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' also said, in distinguishing between them: *al-kurh* (with a *ḍamma*) is what a person imposes upon himself, and with a *fatḥa* is what is imposed upon another, that is, by compulsion and usurpation. For this reason some scholars of Arabic said that *karhan* (with a *fatḥa* on the *kāf*) is a grammatical error.

**Fourth issue:** His saying: ﴿And his bearing and his weaning is thirty months﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: If she carried him for nine months, she nursed him for twenty-one months; if she carried him for six months, she nursed him for twenty-four months. It is narrated that ʿUthman was brought a woman who had given birth after six months, and he intended to pass the *ḥadd* punishment upon her. ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him: "That is not upon her. Allah says: ﴿And his bearing and his weaning is thirty months﴾, and He says: ﴿And mothers suckle their children for two full years﴾ [al-Baqara: 233]. So nursing is twenty-four months and gestation is six months." Then ʿUthman retracted his statement and did not punish her. This has already passed in al-Baqara [see vol. 3, p. 160 and following].

It is also said that the three months at the beginning of the pregnancy were not counted, because during them the child is a drop (*nuṭfa*), a clot (*ʿalaqa*), and a lump of flesh (*muḍgha*), so it has no weight that is felt. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿When he covered her, she bore a light burden, and went about with it﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 189] [Verse 189, Surah al-Aʿraf].

*Al-fiṣāl* is weaning. The discussion of it has already passed in Luqman [see vol. 14, p. 64 and following]. Al-Hasan, Yaʿqub and others read *wa-faṣluhu* with a *fatḥa* on the *fa'* and a sukun on the *ṣād*.

It is narrated that the verse was revealed about Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and that his bearing and weaning were thirty months: his mother carried him for nine months and nursed him for twenty-one months.

In the sentence there is an implied element, that is, "and the period of his bearing and the period of his weaning is thirty months." Were it not for this implied element, *thirty* would be in the accusative as an adverbial of time, and the meaning would change.

**Fifth issue:** His saying: ﴿Until, when he reaches his full strength (*ashuddahu*)﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: eighteen years. In the narration of ʿAtaʾ from him: Abu Bakr accompanied the Prophet ﷺ when he was eighteen years old and the Prophet ﷺ was twenty years old, and they were heading to Syria for trade. They stopped at a place where there was a lote tree, and the Prophet ﷺ sat in its shade. Abu Bakr went to a monk there and asked him about religion. The monk said: "Who is the man who is in the shade of the tree?" He said: "That is Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib." He said: "By Allah, this is a prophet, and no one has sheltered beneath it after ʿIsa." Certainty and belief entered the heart of Abu Bakr, and he hardly ever left the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, on his journeys and at home. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was commissioned as a prophet at the age of forty, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, confirmed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at the age of thirty-eight. When he reached forty he said: "My Lord, grant me inspiration that I may be thankful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents," and the verse.

Al-Shaʿbi and Ibn Zayd said: *al-Ashudd* is maturity of judgement (*al-ḥulm*). Al-Hasan said: it is reaching forty. And from him: the establishment of proof upon him. The discussion of the verse has already passed in al-Anʿam [see vol. 7, p. 134 and following].

Al-Suddi and al-Ḍaḥḥak said: it was revealed about Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas. This has already passed.

Al-Hasan said: it is *mursala* (a report without a link to the Companion), revealed in general terms. And Allah knows best.

**Sixth issue:** His saying: ﴿He said: "My Lord, grant me inspiration"﴾, that is, inspire me. ﴿That I may be thankful﴾ is in the accusative position as a verbal noun, meaning the thanks for Your favour. ﴿Which You have bestowed upon me﴾, that is, what You have bestowed upon me of guidance. ﴿And upon my parents﴾, with tenderness and compassion, until they raised me when I was small. It is said: You have favoured me with health and well-being, and my parents with wealth and abundance.

ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: This verse was revealed about Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. Both his parents embraced Islam, and it was not gathered for any of the Muhajirun that both his parents embraced Islam except him, so Allah enjoined him concerning them, and that obligation remained for those after him. His father was Abu Quhafa ʿUthman ibn ʿAmir ibn ʿAmr ibn Kaʿb ibn Saʿd ibn Taym. His mother was Umm al-Khayr, whose name was Salma bint Sakhr ibn ʿAmir ibn Kaʿb ibn Saʿd. The mother of his father Abu Quhafa was *Qayla* (with a *yāʾ* with two dots below it). The wife of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, whose name was *Qutayla* (with a *tāʾ* with two dots above it), was the daughter of ʿAbd al-ʿUzza.

﴿And that I may do righteous deeds with which You are pleased﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: So Allah answered him, and he freed nine believers who were being tortured for the sake of Allah, among them Bilal and ʿAmir ibn Fuhayra, and he did not leave any good thing except that Allah helped him to do it.

In the Sahih, on the authority of Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Who among you has fasted today?" Abu Bakr said: "I." He said: "Who among you has followed a funeral today?" Abu Bakr said: "I." He said: "Who among you has fed a poor man today?" Abu Bakr said: "I." He said: "Who among you has visited a sick person today?" Abu Bakr said: "I." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "These do not gather in a man except that he enters Paradise."

**Seventh issue:** His saying: ﴿And make my offspring righteous for me﴾, that is, make my offspring righteous. Ibn ʿAbbas said: So no child, parent, or mother remained except that they believed in Allah alone. None of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ embraced Islam with his parents, his children and his daughters all together except Abu Bakr.

Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah said: the meaning is: make them a true successor for me, and servants of truth for You. Abu ʿUthman said: make them dutiful to me, obedient to You. Ibn ʿAta said: grant them success in righteous deeds with which You are pleased with them. Muhammad ibn ʿAli said: do not let Satan, the self, or desire have any way over them. Malik ibn Mighwal said: Abu Maʿshar complained to Talha ibn Musarrif about his son, and he said: "Seek help against him with this verse," and he recited: "My Lord, grant me inspiration that I may be thankful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and that I may do righteous deeds with which You are pleased, and make my offspring righteous for me. Indeed I have turned to You in repentance, and indeed I am of the Muslims."

﴿Indeed I have turned to You in repentance﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: I have returned from the matter in which I was. ﴿And indeed I am of the Muslims﴾, that is, the sincere in monotheism.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verse 16:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those are the ones from whom We accept the best of what they have done and overlook their misdeeds﴾. The recitation of the common readers (al-'Amma) is with a damma on the yā' in both verbs. It is also read "yataqabbalu, wa-yatajawazu" with a fatha on the yā', and the pronoun in both refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Hafs, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "nataqabbalu, wa-natajawazu" with the nūn in both, meaning We forgive them and pardon them. Al-tajawuz (overlooking) is originally from "jurtu al-shay'" (I passed over the thing) when you do not stop at it. This verse indicates that the verse before it, "And We have enjoined upon man" through to its end, is unrestricted and was revealed in general terms, and this is the view of al-Hasan. The meaning of "nataqabbalu 'anhum" is: We accept from them the good deeds and overlook the bad deeds. Zayd ibn Aslam said, relating it as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report: when they embrace Islam, their good deeds are accepted and their bad deeds are forgiven. It has also been said: "the best" (al-ahsan) refers to acts of obedience that merit reward, and there is no reward or punishment attached to the permissible good (al-hasan al-mubah); this was related by Ibn 'Isa. "Among the companions of the Garden" (fi ashab al-jannah): "fi" here carries the sense of "ma'a" (with), meaning "with the companions of the Garden." You say: "He honored you and was kind to you among all the people of the town," meaning "with all of them." "A true promise" (wa'd al-sidq) is in the accusative because it is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) for what precedes it, meaning: Allah promised the people of faith that He would accept the good from their doers of good and overlook the misdeeds of their wrongdoers, as a true promise. This is an instance of the attribution of a thing to itself (idafat al-shay' ila nafsih), because "the truth" is that very promise which Allah made, and it is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the certain truth﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 95]. This is the view of the Kufans; as for the Basrans, its implied sense is: "the promise of the true word" or "the true book," and the qualified noun has been omitted. This has passed in more than one place [see vol. 9, p. 356]. "Which they were promised" in the world through the tongues of the messengers, and that is the Garden.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verse 17–18:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And one who says to his parents, "Uff to you both! Do you promise me that I will be brought forth"﴾, i.e., that I will be resurrected. "And generations have passed away before me" — the reading of Nafi', Hafs and others is "Uff" with a kasra and tanwin. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn 'Amir and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "Uff" with a fatha and without tanwin. The rest read it with a kasra without tanwin, and all of these are dialectal variants (lughat), and this has already been discussed in "Bani Isra'il" [[See vol. 10, p. 242.]]. The common reading of "ataʻidanini" is with two light nuns. The people of Madina and Makka pronounced its ya' with a fatha, and the rest with sukun. Abu Haywa, al-Mughira and Hisham read "ataʻiddanni" with a single doubled nun, and likewise it is in the Mushafs of the people of al-Sham. The common reading of "an ukhraja" is with a damma on the alif and a fatha on the ra'. Al-Hasan, Nasr, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-A'mash and Abu Ma'mar read it with a fatha on the alif and a damma on the ra'.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, Abu al-'Aliyah and Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both. His parents would call him to Islam, and he would answer them with what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has told of. Qatadah and al-Suddi also said: it refers to 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr before his conversion to Islam, and his father and mother, Umm Ruman, would call him to Islam and promise him resurrection, and he would reply to them with what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has related of him, and this was from him before his conversion. It is narrated that 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, denied that it was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman. Al-Hasan and Qatadah also said: it describes a disbelieving servant who disobeys his parents. Al-Zajjaj said: how can it be said that it was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman before his conversion, when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Those are the ones against whom the Word has been justified among nations﴾, meaning the punishment, and it necessarily entails non-belief, whereas 'Abd al-Rahman is among the most excellent of the believers. Therefore the correct view is that it was revealed concerning a disbelieving servant who disobeys his parents. Muhammad ibn Ziyad said: Mu'awiyah wrote to Marwan ibn al-Hakam ordering him to make the people pledge allegiance to Yazid. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr said: You have brought in this Heraclian (hirqliyyah) practice [[He meant that the pledge of allegiance to the sons of kings is the custom of the kings of Rome, and Heraclius was the name of the king of Rome.]]; do you pledge allegiance to your sons! Marwan said: It is he about whom Allah says, "And one who says to his parents, 'Uff to you both'" and the verse. He said: By Allah, it is not he. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And one who says to his parents, "Uff to you both! Do you promise me that I will be brought forth"﴾, i.e., that I will be resurrected. "And generations have passed away before me" — the reading of Nafi', Hafs and others is "Uff" with a kasra and tanwin. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn 'Amir and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "Uff" with a fatha and without tanwin. The rest read it with a kasra without tanwin, and all of these are dialectal variants (lughat), and this has already been discussed in "Bani Isra'il" [[See vol. 10, p. 242.]]. Abu Haywa, al-Mughira and Hisham read "ataʻiddanni" with a single doubled nun, and likewise it is in the Mushafs of the people of al-Sham. Al-Hasan and Qatadah also said: it describes a disbelieving servant who disobeys his parents. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verse 19:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for each there are degrees﴾, meaning: for each one of the two groups, the believers and the disbelievers, among the jinn and mankind, there are ranks with Allah on the Day of Resurrection according to their deeds. Ibn Zayd said: "The degrees of the people of the Fire in this verse go downward (safalan), and the degrees of the people of Paradise go upward (uluwwan)." ﴿And that He may fully pay them their deeds﴾: Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with the yā' (yuwaffiyahum), because of the mention of Allah before it, which is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾. Abu Hatim chose this reading. The rest read it with the nūn (nuwaffiyahum), in response to His saying, may He be exalted: "And We have enjoined upon man (goodness) to his parents" (46:15). This is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾, meaning: nothing will be added to the evil-doer's (sins), nor will anything be diminished from the good-doer's (reward).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verse 20:

Allah's words: ﴿And on the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire﴾. That is, remind them, O Muhammad, of the Day when they are exposed. "To the Fire" means the veil is removed, so they are brought near the Fire and look at it. "You squandered your good things" means it will be said to them, "You squandered," so the saying is implied. Al-Hasan, Nasr, Abu al-'Aliya, Ya'qub and Ibn Kathir read *a-dhhabtum* with two lightened hamzas, and Abu Hatim chose this reading. Abu Haywa and Hisham read *ādhhabtum* with one hamza and a prolonged vowel, as an interrogative (istifham, a question). The rest read it with one hamza and no prolongation, as a declarative (khabar, statement). All of these are eloquent dialectal forms, and their meaning is rebuke. The Arabs rebuke both with the interrogative and without it, as has already been mentioned. Abu 'Ubayd chose the omission of the interrogative, because it is the reading of most of the leading readers of the Seven: Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i, along with those who agreed with them: Shayba, al-Zuhri, Ibn Muhaysin, al-Mughira ibn Abi Shihab, Yahya ibn al-Harith, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab and others. These are the foremost of the people of this reading. Omitting the interrogative is better, because affirming it gives the impression that they did not do that, as when you say, "Did I wrong you?" meaning "I did not wrong you." Affirming it is also acceptable. The speaker says, "You went and did such-and-such," rebuking, and says, "Did you go and do such-and-such!" All of this is permissible.

The meaning of "you squandered your good things" is that you enjoyed good things in the world and followed desires and pleasures, meaning sins. "So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation" means the punishment of disgrace and exposure. Mujahid said: *al-hawn* is *al-hawan* (humiliation). Qatada said: it is in the language of Quraysh. ﴿Because you were arrogant in the earth without right﴾ means you were presumptuous over its people without entitlement. ﴿And because you used to defy﴾ means in your actions, through transgression and wrongdoing.

It has also been said that "you squandered your good things" means you spent your youth in disbelief and sins. Ibn Bahr said: *al-tayyibat* are youth and strength, derived from the saying of people, "His *atyabān* went," meaning his youth and his strength. Al-Mawardi said: I found that al-Dahhak also said this. I say: the first view is more apparent. Al-Hasan narrated from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays that he heard 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, say: "I am more knowledgeable about easy living. Had I wished, I would have made *akbad* (liver dishes), *sila'* (roasted meat), *sinab* (sauces) and *sala'iq* (flatbreads). But I preserve my good deeds, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, described some peoples, saying: ﴿You squandered your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them﴾." Abu 'Ubayd said in the hadith of 'Umar: "Had I wished, I would have called for *sala'iq*, *sinab*, *karakir* and *asnima*." In some narrations there is also *afla*dh. Abu 'Amr and others said: *al-sila'* (with a long vowel and a kasra) is roast meat, named so because it is roasted over fire. *Al-sila'* also means the heat of fire, and if you open the *sad* you shorten it and say *salā al-nār* (he was roasted by the fire). *Al-sinab* is the sauces made from mustard and raisins. Abu 'Amr said: for this reason a horse of a particular colour is called *sinabi*, because its colour is likened to that. He said: *al-sala'iq* (with a *sin*) is what is boiled of greens and other things. Others said: they are *al-sala'iq* with a *sad*. Jarir said:

*You burden me with the livelihood of the family of Zayd,*
*And who am I to afford the flatbreads and the sauces?*

*Al-sala'iq* are thin, wide breads. This meaning has already passed in (al-A'raf) [see vol. 7, p. 198]. As for *al-karakir*, they are the knees (or cartilage) of camels, singular *kirkira*, which is well known; this is the statement of Abu 'Ubayd. In al-Sihah: *al-kirkira* is the cartilage of the camel's chest, and it is one of the five stomachs. *Al-kirkira* also means a group of people. Abu Malik 'Amr ibn Kirkira was a man of the scholars of language. Abu 'Ubayd said: as for *al-afla*dh, its singular is *fild*, which is a piece of liver. A'sha Bahila said:

*A slice of fild from the roast suffices him, if he comes upon it,*
*And the small cup (ghamr) quenches his drink.*

Qatada said: It was mentioned to us that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Had I wished, I would have been the best of you in food and the softest of you in clothing. But I save my good things for the Hereafter." When 'Umar arrived in Syria, a food was prepared for him which he had never seen the like of. He said: "This is for us! Then what of the poor Muslims who died and never had their fill of barley bread?" Khalid ibn al-Walid said: "They have Paradise." 'Umar's eyes welled up with tears and he said: "If our share of this world is this debris, and they have gone with their share in Paradise, then they have left us far behind."

In Sahih Muslim and others, it is narrated that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, entered upon the Prophet ﷺ while he was in his *mashraba* (upper room) when he had abandoned his wives. He said: "I looked around and saw nothing that could catch the eye except *uhub* (hides), *julud* (skins) tanned, whose smell was pungent. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you are the Messenger of Allah and His chosen one, and this is Kisra and Caesar in brocade and silk?' He sat up and said: '*Afi shakkin anta ya ibn al-Khattab?* Those are a people whose good things were hastened for them in their worldly life.'" I said: "Ask forgiveness for me!" He said: "O Allah, forgive him."

Hafs ibn Abi al-'As said: I used to have my midday meal with 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, bread and olive oil, bread and vinegar, bread and milk, bread and *qadid* (dried meat), and the least of it was fresh meat (*al-ghariḍ*, fresh). He used to say: "Do not sift the flour, for it is all food." Then a thick, cracked bread was brought, and he began to eat and say: "Eat!" We did not eat, so he said: "What is wrong with you, that you do not eat?" We said: "By Allah, O Commander of the Faithful, we are going back to food softer than this food of yours!" He said: "O son of Abi al-'As, do you not see that I know that if I ordered a fat young goat to be brought, its hair removed, then it came out roasted looking like such-and-such? Do you not see that I know that if I ordered a *sa'* or two *sa's* of raisins to be put in a waterskin, then water poured over them, it would become in the morning like the blood of a gazelle?" I said: "O Commander of the Faithful, indeed you describe the life of ease!" He said: "Indeed! By Allah, besides whom there is no god, were it not that I fear my good deeds will be diminished on the Day of Resurrection, we would have shared the life of ease with you! But I heard Allah, Mighty and Majestic, say to some peoples: ﴿You squandered your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them﴾."

﴿So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾ means the humiliation. ﴿Because you were arrogant in the earth without right﴾ means you exalted yourselves against obedience to Allah and over the servants of Allah. ﴿And because you used to defy﴾ means you departed from obedience to Allah.

Jabir said: My family desired meat, so I bought it for them. I passed by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said: "What is this, O Jabir?" I informed him, and he said: "Whenever one of you desires something, does he put it in his belly? Does he not fear that he is among the people of this verse: ﴿You squandered your good things﴾, the verse." Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is a reproach from him to Jabir for the extravagance of buying meat and departing from the plain bread and water. Indeed, pursuing the good things of what is lawful makes the natures eager for them and the habit makes them palatable, so when one is deprived of them one finds it easy to obtain them through doubtful matters, until one falls into what is entirely unlawful through the dominance of habit and the craving of desire over the commanding self. So 'Umar took the matter from its beginning and guarded it from its start, as one like him would do. What governs this chapter and preserves its rule is this: a person should eat what he finds, whether it is good or plain (*qifar*, bread without condiment), and should not burden himself with the good nor make it a habit. The Prophet ﷺ would be satisfied when he found food, would be patient when he lacked it, would eat sweets when he was able to, would drink honey when it happened to be available, would eat meat when it was easy to get, but he never relied on it at all, nor made it a constant practice. The Prophet's ﷺ way of life is known, and the way of the Companions is transmitted. As for today, with the dominance of the unlawful and the corruption of worldly goods, deliverance is difficult, but Allah grants sincerity and helps toward deliverance by His mercy.

It has also been said that the rebuke falls upon the abandonment of gratitude, not upon taking the lawful good things. This is a fine view, for taking the lawful good is permitted. If someone does not give thanks for it, and uses it to help himself in what is unlawful for him, then he has squandered it. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verse 21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And mention the brother of ʿAd﴾ is Hud ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Rabah (peace be upon him). He was their brother in lineage, not in religion. ﴿When he warned his people in al-Ahqaf﴾ meaning: mention to these polytheists the story of ʿAd, so that they may take a lesson from it. It was also said: He was commanded to recall in himself the story of Hud, so that he might follow his example and so that the denial of his people would be easier for him to bear.

Al-Ahqaf (the sing. being al-hiqf, the plural being ahqaf) are the dwellings of ʿAd, and they are the great sand dunes, according to al-Khalil and others. They had subdued the people of the earth by the excess of their strength. Al-Ahqaf is the plural of hiqf, which is what extends long from the great sand and bends, without reaching the state of being a mountain; its plurals are hiqaf, ahqaf, and huquf. One says: the sand and the crescent moon "ihqawqafa", meaning it bent. It was also said: hiqf is the plural of hiqaf, and al-ahqaf is the plural of the plural. It is said: hiqf ahqaf. Al-Aʿsha said:

"Bat ila artatin hiqfun ahqafa" [[This verse was attributed by al-Tabari in his tafsir to al-Ajjaj, and we have not found it in the poetry of al-Aʿsha nor in the rajaz of al-Ajjaj. Artah: its plural is artY, a tree of the sandy desert.]]

meaning a long, raised sand dune. Its verb is ihqawqafa. Al-Ajjaj said:

"Ṭayy al-layali zulafan fa-zulafa ... samawat al-hilal hatta ihqawqafa"

meaning it bent and curved. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Ka-hiqfi al-naqa yamshi al-walidani fawqahu ... bima ihtasaba min layyin massin wa tashhal"

[[al-Naqa: a sand dune.]]

Regarding what is meant by al-Ahqaf here, there is disagreement. Ibn Zayd said: they are long, raised sand dunes like the shape of mountains, but they did not reach being mountains, and his proof is what we have mentioned. Qatadah said: they are raised mountains in al-Shihr, and al-Shihr is near ʿAdan; it is said: Shihr ʿUman and Shihr ʿAmman, and it is the sea coast between ʿUman and ʿAdan. Also from him: it was mentioned to us that ʿAd were living in Yemen, a people of sand overlooking the sea in a land called al-Shihr. Mujahid said: it is a land from Hismá called al-Ahqaf. Hismá (with a kasra on the ha') is the name of a land in the desert containing high mountains with smooth sides, which the dust hardly leaves. Al-Nabigha said:

"Fa-asbaha ʿaqilan bi-jibali Hismá ... duqaqa al-turbi muhtazima al-qatam"

[[Ibn Barri said: "i.e., Hismá, around which the dust surrounds like a belt for it."]]

So said al-Jawhari. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak said: al-Ahqaf is a mountain in al-Sham. Also from Ibn ʿAbbas: a valley between ʿUman and Mahrah. Muqatil said: the dwellings of ʿAd were in Yemen, in Hadramawt, in a valley called Mahrah, and the Mahri camels are attributed to it, so one says: Mahri camels and mahari. They were people of mobile pillars in spring; when the herbage dried, they returned to their dwellings. They were from the tribe of Iram. Al-Kalbi said: the ahqaf of the mountain are what the water recedes from in the time of the flood; the water would recede from the earth and its trace would remain.

Al-Tufayl narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: The best of the two valleys among people is a valley in Mecca and a valley where Adam settled in the land of India. The worst of the two valleys among people is a valley in al-Ahqaf and a valley in Hadramawt called Barhut, where the souls of the disbelievers are cast. The best well among people is the well of Zamzam, and the worst well among people is the well of Barhut, which is in that valley in Hadramawt.

﴿And warners had passed﴾ meaning the messengers had passed away. ﴿Before him and after him﴾ meaning before Hud and after him, as said by al-Farra'. In the recitation of Ibn Masʿud: "min bayni yadayhi wa min baʿdihi". ﴿That you worship none but Allah﴾ This is from the speech of the messenger, so it is an interjected statement. Then Hud said: ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a great day.﴾ It was also said that "that you worship none but Allah" is from the speech of Hud. And Allah knows best.

﴿They said, "Have you come to us to turn us away from our gods?"﴾ In this there are two interpretations. The first: to remove us from worshipping them through falsehood. The second: to divert us from our gods by prohibiting us; this is the view of al-Dahhak. ʿUrwa ibn Udhayna said:

"If you are not granted success in the best of deeds,
then you are among others who have been turned away."

He means: if you are not granted success in doing good, then you are among a people who have been diverted.

"Bring us what you promise us." This shows that a promise (waʿd) may be used in place of a threat (waʿīd).

"If you are among the truthful," that you are a prophet. ﴿He said, "Knowledge is only with Allah."﴾ That is, knowledge of the time when the punishment will come is with Allah, not with me. ﴿"And I convey to you what I have been sent with,"﴾ from your Lord. ﴿"But I see you as a people who are ignorant."﴾ In your asking for the punishment to be hastened.

﴿So when they saw it as a cloud spreading across the sky,﴾ al-Mubarrad said: the pronoun in "raʾawhu" (they saw it) refers to something not mentioned, and its explanation is the phrase "ʿāriḍan" (a cloud spreading across the sky). So the pronoun refers to the cloud, meaning: when they saw the cloud spreading across the sky. "ʿāriḍan" is in the accusative as a repetition (takrīr) of the object. It was so named because it appears across the breadth of the sky. It was also said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

It was also said that the pronoun refers to the phrase "Bring us what you promise us." So when they saw it, they thought it was a cloud that would bring them rain, and rain had been delayed from them. When they saw it ﴿coming towards their valleys﴾ they rejoiced. It had come to them from a valley from which it was customary that whatever came would bring rain. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and others.

Al-Jawhari said: "al-ʿāriḍ" is a cloud that spreads across the horizon. From this is the verse ﴿"This is a cloud bringing us rain,"﴾ meaning a cloud that brings rain to us. It is definite (maʿrifa), and it is not permissible for it to be an adjective of "ʿāriḍ," which is indefinite (nakira). The Arabs only do this with derived nouns (ism mushtaqq) derived from verbs, and not otherwise. Jarir said:

"O how often one who envied us, if he had been seeking you,
would have met with distance from you and deprivation."

It is not permissible to say: "This is the man of our boy." An Arab said after the Fitr (end of Ramadan): "How many a woman fasting who will not fast it, and a woman standing in prayer who will not stand it." He made it an adjective for an indefinite noun and attributed it to a definite noun.
