﴿So when they saw it as a cloud spreading across the sky,﴾ al-Mubarrad said: the pronoun in "raʾawhu" (they saw it) refers to something not mentioned, and its explanation is the phrase "ʿāriḍan" (a cloud spreading across the sky). So the pronoun refers to the cloud, meaning: when they saw the cloud spreading across the sky. "ʿāriḍan" is in the accusative as a repetition (takrīr) of the object. It was so named because it appears across the breadth of the sky. It was also said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

It was also said that the pronoun refers to the phrase "Bring us what you promise us." So when they saw it, they thought it was a cloud that would bring them rain, and rain had been delayed from them. When they saw it ﴿coming towards their valleys﴾ they rejoiced. It had come to them from a valley from which it was customary that whatever came would bring rain. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and others.

Al-Jawhari said: "al-ʿāriḍ" is a cloud that spreads across the horizon. From this is the verse ﴿"This is a cloud bringing us rain,"﴾ meaning a cloud that brings rain to us. It is definite (maʿrifa), and it is not permissible for it to be an adjective of "ʿāriḍ," which is indefinite (nakira). The Arabs only do this with derived nouns (ism mushtaqq) derived from verbs, and not otherwise. Jarir said:

"O how often one who envied us, if he had been seeking you,
would have met with distance from you and deprivation."

It is not permissible to say: "This is the man of our boy." An Arab said after the Fitr (end of Ramadan): "How many a woman fasting who will not fast it, and a woman standing in prayer who will not stand it." He made it an adjective for an indefinite noun and attributed it to a definite noun.

I say: his saying, "It is not permissible for it to be an adjective of ʿāriḍ," contradicts the view of the grammarians (naḥwiyyūn). The construction (iḍāfa) is considered as separated, so it is a verbal construction (iḍāfa lafẓiyya), not a true construction (ḥaqīqiyya), because it does not make the first noun definite. Rather, the noun remains indefinite in its state, and therefore it functions as an adjective of an indefinite noun. This is the view of the grammarians regarding the verse and the line of poetry. And the adjective of an indefinite noun is indefinite. "Rubba" (how many) only enters upon an indefinite noun.

﴿"Rather, it is what you were hastening for,"﴾ that is, Hud said to them. The evidence for this is the reading of the one who reads "Hud said, 'Rather, it is,'" and the reading "Say: 'Rather, what you were hastening for is a wind in which is a painful punishment.'" That is, Allah said: "Say, 'Rather, it is what you were hastening for,'" meaning their saying: "Bring us what you promise us." Then He explained what it was, saying: ﴿"a wind in which is a painful punishment."﴾

The wind by which they were punished arose from that cloud they had seen. Hud had gone out from among them. It began to carry the tents and carry the camel-litter (ẓaʿīna), [[The ẓaʿīna is the camel that is ridden, on which a litter is carried, whether or not there is a woman in the litter.]] lifting it up like a locust, then striking it against the rocks.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: When they first saw the cloud, they stood up and stretched out their hands. What first made them realize it was a punishment was that they saw what had been outside their homes, men and livestock, being carried by the wind between heaven and earth like feathers. So they entered their houses and closed their doors. The wind uprooted the doors and felled them. Allah commanded the wind, and it piled the sand upon them. They remained under the sand for seven nights and eight days, continuous days, [[The "ayyām ḥusūm" are days of continuous (uninterrupted) harm among people.]] and they were moaning. Then Allah commanded the wind, and it cleared the sand away from them, carried them, and threw them into the sea. This is what Allah the Exalted referred to when He said: ﴿"destroying everything by the command of its Lord,"﴾ meaning everything it passed over of the men of ʿĀd and their property.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: that is, everything it was sent to. Al-tadmīr is destruction, and likewise al-damār. It is read "yudammir kulla shay'" from dammara, damāran. It is said: "dammarahu tadmīran wa damāran" and "dammara ʿalayhi" with the same meaning. And "damara yadmuru dumūran" means he entered without permission. In a hadith: "Whoever his glance precedes his seeking permission has entered without permission" (damara), with the letter mīm lightened. Tudmur is a town in Syria. And a "yarbūʿ tudmurī" is a small short man.

﴿"by the command of its Lord"﴾ means by the permission of its Lord.

In Bukhari, from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), she said: "I never saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughing so that I could see his uvula (lahawāt) [[Plural of lahāh, which is the fleshy part projecting over the throat at the farthest part of the roof of the mouth.]]. He only smiled." She said: "When he saw a cloud or a wind, it was recognized in his face." She said: "O Messenger of Allah, people when they see the clouds rejoice, hoping that there will be rain in it, and I see you when you see it, the dislike is recognized in your face?" He said: "O ʿĀʾisha, what assures me that it does not contain a punishment? A people were punished with the wind, and a people saw the punishment and said, 'This is a cloud bringing us rain.'" [Recorded by Muslim and al-Tirmidhi, who said regarding it: "a good (ḥasan) hadith." In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "I have been supported with the eastern wind (al-ṣabā), and ʿĀd were destroyed with the western wind (al-dabūr)."] [[Al-ṣabā (with fatḥa): the north wind. Al-dabūr: the south wind.]]

Al-Mawardi mentioned that the one who said "This is a cloud bringing us rain" was from the people of ʿĀd: Bakr ibn Muʿawiya. When he saw the cloud he said: "Indeed I see a cloud that is burnt (murammad), it leaves nothing of ʿĀd behind." [[In the Nihāya of Ibn al-Athīr and the Lisān, under the root (r-m-d), and the Tārīkh of al-Ṭabarī: "Take it as ashes, reduced to ashes, it leaves none of ʿĀd." Al-ramad (with kasra): that which is extremely burnt and fine.]]

ʿAmr ibn Maymun mentioned that the wind would bring to them the man who was absent, until it threw him into their assembly. Ibn Ishaq said: Hud and those believers with him withdrew into an enclosure, and what touched him and those with him from it was only what softened the upper parts of their garments, and their souls found pleasure in it. And indeed the wind passed over ʿĀd carrying the camel-litters between heaven and earth, and it struck them with stones until they perished.

Al-Kalbi related that their poet said regarding that:

"Hud invoked against them
an invocation that left them silent (humūdan),
a wind blew upon them,
which left ʿĀd extinguished (khumūdan),
it was subjugated for seven nights,
it left no tree in the land (ʿūdan)."

Hud lived among his people after them for one hundred and fifty years.

﴿So they became such that nothing could be seen except their dwellings.﴾ ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza read "lā yurā illā masākinuhum" with a yāʾ, not naming the subject. Likewise Ḥammād ibn Salama related from Ibn Kathīr, except that he read "turā" with a tāʾ. This was also related from Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim. The rest read "tarā" with an open tāʾ. "Masākinuhum" is in the nominative case (in this reading of the rest it is accusative: "masākinahum"). Meaning: "Lā tarā yā Muḥammad illā masākinahum" (you do not see, O Muhammad, except their dwellings).

Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads with tāʾ without naming the subject, then it is according to the apparent wording, which is the feminine dwellings, and this is rare, used only in poetry. Abū Ḥātim said: this is not correct in the language except that there is an implied element in it, as you say in speech: "Alā turā al-nisāʾ illā Zaynab," and it is not permissible to say: "Lā turā illā Zaynab."

Sibawayh said: its meaning is: their persons are not seen except their dwellings. Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred the reading of ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza. Al-Kisāʾī said: its meaning is: nothing is seen except their dwellings, so it is understood according to the sense, as you say: "Mā qāma illā Hind," and the meaning is "No one stood except Hind." Al-Farrāʾ said: the people are not seen because they were under the sand, and only their dwellings are seen because they are standing.

﴿Thus do We recompense the criminal people.﴾ That is, We punish the polytheists with the like of this punishment.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 46, verse 26:**

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And We had certainly established them in that wherein We have established you﴾. It has been said that *in* (*in*) is redundant (*za'ida*), its meaning being: "And We had certainly established them in that wherein We have established you." This is the view of al-Qutabi. Al-Akhfash cited:

*"A man hopes for what he does not see [in*, i.e., *ma in*] ... and calamities stand between him and its nearest approach."*

Another poet said:

*"Our disposition is not cowardice, but our fates and the state of others [who came after us]."* [[The verse is by Farwa ibn Musayk al-Muradi. *Tabb* means: matter, custom, desire and will.]]

It has also been said that *ma* means *alladhi* (that which), and *in* means *ma* (what not), and the meaning is: "And We had certainly established them in that which We did not establish you in." This was stated by al-Mubarrad.

It has been said that *in* is conditional (*shartiyya*), and its answer is an implied, omitted response. The meaning is: "And We had certainly established them in that wherein, if We had established you in it, your transgression would have been greater and your obstinacy more intense." The sentence is complete there. Then he began anew, saying: ﴿And We made for them hearing and sight and hearts﴾, meaning hearts by which they understand. ﴿But their hearing did not avail them, nor their sight, nor their hearts, in anything﴾, meaning from the punishment of Allah, ﴿since they used to deny the signs of Allah﴾, meaning they disbelieved in them, ﴿and there encompassed them﴾, meaning surrounded them, ﴿that which they used to mock.﴾

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had destroyed the towns around you﴾. He means the dwelling-place of Thamud (Hijr), the towns of Lut, and others like them that bordered the land of the Hijaz, and whose reports were widely transmitted among them.

"And We diversified the signs" means the proofs, the indications, the various kinds of clear evidence and admonitions; that is, We made them clear to the people of those towns. ﴿So that they might return﴾, but they did not return.

It has also been said: that is, We diversified the verses of the Qur'an in promise and threat, in narratives and in its inimitability, so that perhaps these polytheists would return.

**Qur'an 46:28:** ﴿So why did they not get help from those they had taken as gods, instead of God?﴾

Allah's words, "*fa-lawla nasarahum*" ("so why did they not help them?"): *fa-lawla* has the sense of *halla* ("why not"), meaning: why did their gods not help them, those through which they sought nearness to God according to their claim, that they might intercede for them, as they said: ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus 10:18] "and protect them from the destruction that befell them." Al-Kisa'i (the grammarian and Qur'an reader) said: *al-qurban* is everything by which one draws near to God Most High, whether obedience or sacrifice. Its plural is *qarabin*, like *ruhban* and *rahabin*.

One of the two objects of *ittakhadha* (took) is the returning pronoun [[Footnote in source: the pronoun referring back]] to *alladhina* (those), which is elided, and the second is *alihatan* (gods). *Qurbanan* is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), and it is not valid for *qurbanan* to be the second object. *Alihatan* is a substitute (*badal*) for it, because the meaning would otherwise be corrupted; this is what al-Zamakhshari said. It is also read as *qurubanan* with a *damma* on the *ra'*.

Allah's words, "*bal dallu 'anhum*" ("rather, they went astray from them"): meaning, they were destroyed and lost to them. It was also said: "*dallu 'anhum*" means their gods strayed away from them, because the calamity did not reach them, since they are inanimate. And it was said: "*dallu 'anhum*" means they abandoned the idols and disowned them.

Allah's words, "*wa dhalika ifkuhum*" ("and that was their falsehood"): meaning, and the gods that strayed from them were their falsehood in their claim that they would bring them near to God in closeness. The standard reading is *ifkuhum*, with a *kasra* on the hamza and a sukun on the *fa'*, meaning their lie. *Al-ifk* means falsehood, and so does *al-afika*, whose plural is *al-afa'ik*. A *rajul affak* is a man who is a great liar.

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn al-Zubayr read *wa dhalika afakahum*, with a fatha on the hamza, the fa' and the kaf, as a verb, meaning that this statement turned them away from monotheism. *Al-afk*, with a fatha, is the verbal noun of your saying *afakahu ya'fikuhu afkan*, meaning he turned him and diverted him from a thing.

Ikrimah read *affakahum*, with a shadda on the fa', for emphasis and intensification. Abu Hatim said: he means he turned them away from the bounty they had been in.

Al-Mahdawi also reported from Ibn Abbas *afikahum*, with a long vowel and a kasra on the fa', meaning those who turn them away. From Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, with a variant from him, *afakahum* with a long vowel, which may be *af'alahum*, meaning he made them into falsehood, and may be *fa'alahum*, like *khada'ahum* (he deceived them).

The evidence for the standard reading *ifkuhum* is his words, "*wa ma kanu yaftarun*" ("and what they used to fabricate"), meaning, what they used to lie. It was also said that *ifkuhum* is like *afakahum*. *Al-ifk* and *al-afak* are like *al-hidhr* and *al-hadhar*; this is what al-Mahdawi said.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verse 29 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We directed to you a company of the jinn﴾. This is a rebuke to the polytheists of Quraysh, meaning: the jinn heard the Qur'an, believed in it, and knew that it was from Allah, while you turn away and persist in disbelief. The meaning of "directed" (ṣarafnā) is "turned toward you" and "sent." That is because they were prevented from eavesdropping (istirāq al-sam') from the heaven by meteors (shuhub), as will come, and after 'Isa they had not been prevented from it except at the time of the Prophet's ﷺ mission.

The exegetes Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and others said: When Abu Talib died, the Prophet ﷺ went out alone to Ta'if seeking support from Thaqif. He went to 'Abd Yalil, Mas'ud and Habib, who were brothers, the sons of 'Amr ibn 'Umayr, and with them was a woman of Quraysh from the Banu Jumah. He invited them to faith and asked them to support him against his people. One of them said: "He would tear off the clothes of the Ka'bah if Allah had sent you!" Another said: "Did Allah find no one else to send but you!" The third said: "By Allah, I will never speak to you a single word. If Allah has sent you as you claim, then you are of too great a status for me to answer you, and if you are lying, then it is not fitting for me to speak to you." Then they incited their foolish ones and their slaves against him, cursing him and laughing at him, until people gathered around him and drove him to a wall belonging to 'Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah. He said to the Jumahiyyah: "What have we met from your in-laws?" Then he said: "O Allah, I complain to You of the weakness of my strength, the scarcity of my resources and my humiliation before people. O Most Merciful of the merciful, You are the Lord of the weak, and You are my Lord. To whom will You entrust me? To a stranger who will scowl at me, or to an enemy whom You have given power over my affair? If there is no anger from You upon me, then I do not care, but Your well-being is more expansive for me. I seek refuge in the light of Your face from Your anger descending upon me or Your wrath befalling me. To You is the reproach until You are pleased, and there is no power and no strength except through You."

The two sons of Rabi'ah took pity on him and said to a Christian slave of theirs called 'Addas: "Take a bunch of grapes, put it on this platter, and place it before this man." When he placed it before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the Prophet ﷺ said: "In the name of Allah," and then ate. 'Addas looked at his face and then said: "By Allah, these words are not what the people of this town say!"

The Prophet ﷺ said: "From which lands are you, O 'Addas, and what is your religion?"

He said: "I am a Christian from the people of Nineveh."

The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "From the town of the righteous man, Yunus ibn Matta?"

He said: "And what would make you know of Yunus ibn Matta?"

He said: "That was my brother; he was a prophet, and I am a prophet." Then 'Addas bent down until he kissed the head of the Prophet ﷺ, his hands and his feet.

The two sons of Rabi'ah said to him: "Why did you do that?"

He said: "O my master, there is nothing on earth better than this. He told me of a matter that none knows except a prophet."

Then the Prophet ﷺ left when he despaired of the good of Thaqif. When he reached Batn Nakhlah, he stood up in the night to pray, and a group of jinn from the people of Nasibin passed by him.

The reason for this was that the jinn used to eavesdrop, but when the heaven was guarded and they were pelted with meteors, Iblis said: "What has happened in the heaven is a thing that has happened on earth." So he sent his detachments to learn the news. The first of them was a company from Nasibin, who were the noblest of the jinn, toward Tihamah. When they reached Batn Nakhlah, they heard the Prophet ﷺ praying the dawn prayer at Batn Nakhlah and reciting the Qur'an. They listened to him and said: "Be silent!"

Another group said: "Rather, the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to warn the jinn, invite them to Allah the Exalted, and recite the Qur'an to them. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, directed to him a group of jinn from Nineveh and gathered them for him." The Prophet ﷺ said: "I intend to recite the Qur'an to the jinn tonight. Which of you will follow me?"

They lowered their heads. Then he said it a second time, and they lowered their heads. Then he said it a third time, and they lowered their heads. Ibn Mas'ud said: "I (will), O Messenger of Allah." Ibn Mas'ud said: "No one was present with him except me. We set out until, when we were at the upper part of Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ entered a mountain pass called (Shi'b al-Hajun). He drew a line for me and commanded me to sit within it, and said: 'Do not leave it until I return to you.'"

Then he set off until he stood and began the Qur'an. I began to see things like eagles swooping and walking in their wings, and I heard a clamor and a murmur, until I feared for the Prophet ﷺ. Many shadows (aswidah) surrounded him and came between me and him, until I could no longer hear his voice. Then they began to disperse like pieces of clouds, departing. The Prophet ﷺ finished with the dawn, and said: "Did you sleep?"

I said: "No, by Allah. I had resolved several times to call for help from the people, until I heard you striking them with your staff, saying: 'Sit down!'" He said: "If you had come out, I would not have been safe for you from some of them snatching you away." Then he said: "Did you see anything?"

I said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah. I saw black men with their garments tucked up between their thighs, wearing white clothes." He said: "Those were the jinn of Nasibin. They asked me for provisions and food, so I provided them with every decayed bone and dung and dropping."

They said: "O Messenger of Allah, people will find it filthy for us." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade cleaning oneself with bone and dung.

I said: "O Prophet of Allah, and what benefit is that to them?" He said: "They will not find a bone without finding meat on it on the day it was eaten, nor a dropping without finding its grain in it on the day it was eaten." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, I heard a very loud clamor." He said: "The jinn disputed over a slain man among them, so they came to me for judgment, and I judged between them with truth." Then the Prophet ﷺ relieved himself, then came to me and said: "Do you have any water?" I said: "O Prophet of Allah, I have a small water-skin (idawah) containing some date-wine (nabidh al-tamr)." I poured it over his hands, and he performed ablution, and said: "A good date, and pure water."

Ma'mar narrated its meaning from Qatadah, and Shu'bah also narrated it from Ibn Mas'ud. In the hadith of Ma'mar there is no mention of date-wine.

It is narrated from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi that Ibn Mas'ud saw the Zutt [a dark-skinned people from Sind; it was said: the Arabicized form of "jat" in Hindi, a people from India], and said: "Who are these?" He said: "These are the Zutt." He said: "I have seen nothing resembling them except the jinn on the night of the jinn, for they were restless, one following another."

Al-Daraqutni mentioned from 'Abd Allah ibn Lahi'ah: Qays ibn al-Hajjaj narrated to me from Hansh, from Ibn 'Abbas, from Ibn Mas'ud, that he performed ablution for the Prophet ﷺ on the night of the jinn with date-wine, and he performed ablution with it and said: "It is a drink and a purifier."

Ibn Lahi'ah is not to be relied upon as evidence.

By this same chain from Ibn Mas'ud: he went out with the Prophet ﷺ on the night of the jinn, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "Do you have water, O Ibn Mas'ud?" He said: "I have date-wine in a water-skin." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Pour some of it over me." So he performed ablution and said: "It is a drink and a purifier." Ibn Lahi'ah alone narrated this, and he is weak in hadith.

Al-Daraqutni said: It was also said that Ibn Mas'ud did not witness the night of the jinn with the Prophet ﷺ. Thus 'Alqamah ibn Qays, Abu 'Ubaydah ibn 'Abd Allah and others narrated from him that he said: "I did not witness the night of the jinn."

Abu Muhammad ibn Sa'id narrated to us: Abu al-Ash'ath narrated to us: Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us: Dawud ibn Abi Hind narrated to us, from 'Amir, from 'Alqamah ibn Qays, who said: I said to 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "Did any of you witness the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the night when the caller of the jinn came to him?" He said: "No."

Al-Daraqutni said: This is a sound chain, and there is no disagreement about the trustworthiness of its narrator.

And from 'Amr ibn Murrah, who said: I said to Abu 'Ubaydah: "Did 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud attend the night of the jinn?" He said: "No."

Ibn 'Abbas said: The jinn were seven men from the jinn of Nasibin, and the Prophet ﷺ made them messengers to their people.

Zirr ibn Hubaysh said: They were nine, one of them being Zawba'ah.

Qatadah said: They were from the people of Nineveh.

Mujahid said: From the people of Harran.

'Ikrimah said: From the island of Mosul.

It was also said: They were seven, three from the people of Najran and four from the people of Nasibin.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said in this hadith, mentioning Nasibin: "It was raised to me until I saw it, and I supplicated Allah that its rain be abundant, its trees flourish, and its river be made to flow."

Al-Suhayli said: It is said they were seven, and that they were Jews who then embraced Islam, and for this reason they said: "Revealed after Musa" (Qur'an 46:30).

Names were also given to them: Shasir [in the lexicon: "Shiṣār," with the vowel pattern of "kitāb"], Masir, Mansha, Mashi and al-Ahqab. Ibn Durayd mentioned these five.

Among them was 'Amr ibn Jabir, mentioned by Ibn Sallam through the route of Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i, from his shaykhs, from Ibn Mas'ud, that he was among a group of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ walking, when a whirlwind was lifted up before them, then a greater whirlwind came, and there was a dead snake. A man among us went to his cloak, tore it, shrouded the snake with part of it, and buried it. When night fell, two women came asking: "Which of you buried 'Amr ibn Jabir?" We said: "We do not know who 'Amr ibn Jabir is!" They said: "If you sought reward, you have found it. The wicked jinn fought with the believers, and 'Amr was killed. He is the snake you saw, and he was one of the group who listened to the Qur'an from Muhammad ﷺ, then returned to their people as warners."

Ibn Sallam mentioned another report: that the one who shrouded him was Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal.

I say: al-Tha'labi also mentioned this report in similar words, saying: Thabit ibn Qutbah said: Some people came to Ibn Mas'ud and said: "We were in a journey, and we saw a snake thrashing in its blood. A man among us took it and we buried it. Then some people came and said: 'Which of you buried 'Amr?' We said: 'And who is 'Amr?' They said: 'The snake you buried in such-and-such a place. He was one of the group who heard the Qur'an from the Prophet ﷺ, and there was fighting between two tribes of jinn, Muslims and disbelievers, and he was killed.'"

In this report, Ibn Mas'ud was neither on the journey nor present at the burial, and Allah knows best.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated from a man of the Successors whom he named: that a snake entered upon him in his tent panting from thirst, so he gave it water, then it died, and he buried it. Then at night he was visited, greeted, and thanked, and it was told to him that the snake had been a man from the jinn of Nasibin named Zawba'ah.

Al-Suhayli said: We have been told, regarding the virtues of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah be pleased with him, what Abu Bakr ibn Tahir al-Ishbili narrated to us: that 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz was walking in a barren land, when he found a dead snake. He shrouded it with a remnant of his cloak and buried it. Then a speaker said: "O Surraq, I bear witness that I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'You will die in a barren land, and a righteous man will shroud you.'"

He said: "And who are you, may Allah have mercy on you?"

He said: "A man from the jinn who listened to the Qur'an from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. None of them remains except myself and Surraq, and this Surraq has died."

Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) once killed a snake that she saw in her chamber while she was listening to someone reciting, and Aisha was reciting. She was then shown in a dream, and it was said to her: "You have killed a believing man from among the jinn, those who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." She said: "Had he been a believer, he would not have entered upon me. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade it." It was said to her: "He did not enter upon you except while you were veiled, and he came only to listen to the remembrance." So Aisha woke up frightened, bought slaves and freed them.

Al-Suhayli said: "We have mentioned the names of these jinn that we came across. If they were seven, then al-Ahqab among them is a description of one of them, not a proper name, for the names we mentioned just above number eight, including al-Ahqab."

And Allah knows best.

I say: The memorizer (al-Hafiz) Ibn 'Asakir mentioned in his history:

Hamma ibn al-Haym [[In some manuscripts: "al-Ahyam".]] ibn al-Aqyas ibn Iblis. It has been said that he was one of the believing jinn and among those who met the Prophet ﷺ and was taught by him the Surahs ﴿When the Inevitable Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1], ﴿By the winds sent forth﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1], ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ [al-Naba': 1], ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾ [al-Takwir: 1], ﴿Al-Hamd (The Opening)﴾ [al-Fatihah: 1], and the two refuges ("al-Mu'awwidhatayn") [al-Falaq: 1 and al-Nas: 1].

It is mentioned that he witnessed the killing of Habil (Abel), and took part in his blood, while he was a boy of a few years. It is also mentioned that he met Nuh (Noah), and repented at his hands; and Hud, Salih, Ya'qub (Jacob), Yusuf (Joseph), Ilyas (Elias), Musa ibn 'Imran (Moses son of Imran), and 'Isa ibn Maryam (Jesus son of Mary), peace be upon them all.

Al-Mawardi mentioned their names from Mujahid, saying: Hassa, Massa, Munashsha, Shasir, Masir, al-Arad, Anyan and al-Ahqam.

Abu 'Amr 'Uthman ibn Ahmad, known as Ibn al-Sammak, also mentioned them, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Bara' narrated to us, saying: al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar narrated to us, saying: Hamzah ibn 'Utbah ibn Abi Lahab used to name the jinn of Nasibin who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, saying: Hassa, Massa, Shasir, Masir, al-Afkhar, al-Arad and Anyan. [[We have not been able to verify these names. The manuscripts and sources available to us are confused regarding them.]]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When they attended it﴾, meaning they attended the Prophet ﷺ. This is an instance of shifting the address (talwin al-khitab). It has also been said: when they attended the Qur'an and listened to it. ﴿They said, "Be silent"﴾, meaning some of them said to others: "Be quiet to listen to the Qur'an." Ibn Mas'ud said: They descended upon the Prophet ﷺ while he was reciting the Qur'an in the valley of Nakhlah. When they heard it, "they said, 'Be silent,'" and they said, "Sh!" They were seven, one of whom was Zawba'ah. So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And [mention] when We directed to you a company of the jinn listening to the Qur'an. And when they attended it, they said, "Be silent." And when it was concluded, they went back to their people as warners﴾ up to His saying: ﴿in manifest error﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29–32].

It has also been said that "Be silent" was for hearing the words of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the meanings are close. ﴿When it was concluded﴾. Lahiq ibn Humayd and Khubayb ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr read "fa-lamma qudiya" with a fatha on the qaf and the dad, meaning the Prophet ﷺ, before the prayer. This is because they set out when the sky was guarded against eavesdropping, to find out what had caused this. They came to the valley of Nakhlah while the Prophet ﷺ was reciting in the dawn prayer. They were seven, so they listened to him and returned to their people as warners. The Prophet ﷺ did not know about them.

It has also been said: rather, the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to warn the jinn and recite the Qur'an to them, so Allah turned a company of the jinn toward him to listen to him and warn their people. When he had recited the Qur'an to them and finished, they left at his command, heading to those behind them among their people, the jinn, warning them of opposing the Qur'an and cautioning them about the punishment of Allah if they did not believe. This indicates that they believed in the Prophet ﷺ and that he had sent them. This is supported by their saying: ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah and believe in him﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31]. Had it not been so, they would not have warned their people. It has already been mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet ﷺ made them messengers to their people. Accordingly, the night of the jinn was two nights. This meaning has already been discussed fully. Sahih Muslim contains what supports this, as will be explained in His saying: ﴿Say, "It has been revealed to me"﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]. [[See vol. 19, p. 1.]]

In Sahih Muslim, from Ma'n, who said: I heard my father say: I asked Masruq, "Who informed the Prophet ﷺ about the jinn on the night they listened to the Qur'an?" He said: "Your father, meaning Ibn Mas'ud, told me that a tree informed him of them." [[Adhana: to know.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verse 30–31:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Musa"﴾, meaning the Qur'an. They had been believers in Musa. Ata said: They were Jews and then embraced Islam, and for this reason they said, "revealed after Musa." It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that the jinn had not heard of the matter of Isa, and therefore they said, "revealed after Musa." ﴿Confirming what came before it﴾, meaning what preceded it of the Torah. ﴿It guides to the truth﴾, the religion of truth. ﴿And to a straight path﴾, the upright religion of Allah. ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), and this indicates that he was sent to the jinn and mankind. Muqatil said: Allah did not send a prophet to the jinn and mankind before Muhammad (ﷺ).

I say: This is supported by what is in Sahih Muslim from Jabir ibn Abdullah al-Ansari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been given five things that no one before me was given. Every prophet was sent to his own people specifically, but I have been sent to every red and black (person). Spoils of war have been made lawful for me, though they were not made lawful for anyone before me. The earth has been made for me pure, a means of purification and a place of prostration, so whichever man the prayer overtakes may pray wherever he is. I have been aided with terror striking (the enemy) a month's journey ahead of me, and I have been given intercession." Mujahid said: "the red and the black" means the jinn and mankind. In a narration from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "I have been sent to all creation, and the prophets were sealed with me." ﴿And believe in Him﴾, that is, in the caller, who is Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: "in Him" means in Allah, based on His saying: ﴿He will forgive you some of your sins﴾. Ibn Abbas said: Seventy men from their people responded to them, so they returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and met him at al-Batha'. He recited the Qur'an to them and commanded and forbade them.

Issue: These verses indicate that the jinn are like mankind in commands, prohibitions, reward and punishment. Al-Hasan said: The believing jinn have no reward except their deliverance from the Fire, indicated by His saying: ﴿He will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment﴾. Abu Hanifa also held this view, saying: The reward of the jinn is only that they are protected from the Fire, and then it is said to them: "Be dust like the beasts." Others said: They are recompensed for good deeds just as they are punished for evil deeds, like mankind. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ibn Abi Layla. Al-Dahhak said: The jinn enter Paradise and eat and drink. Al-Qushayri said: The correct position is that this is a matter on which nothing has been decided definitively, and knowledge is with Allah.

I say: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for each there are degrees according to what they did﴾ [al-An'am: 132] indicates that they are rewarded and enter Paradise, because at the beginning of that verse He says: "O assembly of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My verses..." up to His saying: "And for each there are degrees according to what they did" [al-An'am: 130–132]. And Allah knows best. More explanation of this will come, God willing, in Surah al-Rahman.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 46, verse 33:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not seen that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾. The word "seeing" (al-ru'yah) here means knowledge ('ilm). "That" (anna), with its noun and its predicate, takes the place of the two objects of "seeing." ﴿And He was not wearied by their creation, able to give life to the dead﴾ is an argument against those who deny resurrection. The meaning of "lam ya'ya" is that He is not incapable or weakened in originating them. It is said: "'ayya bi-amrihi" and "'iyiya" when one does not find the way to its right course, and the idgham (assimilation) is more common. In the plural one says "'ayyu" (lightened) and also "'ayyu" with shaddah. [A poet said:]

"'Ayyu bi-amrihim kama ... 'ayyat bi-baydatiha al-hamamah"
[The verse is by 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras.]

And: "'Iyitu bi-amri" when you do not find the way to its right course. "A'yani huwa" (it wearied me). Al-Hasan read "wa-lam ya'i" with a kasrah on the 'ayn and sukun on the ya', which is rare and anomalous; the assimilation (i'lal) of the 'ayn with the correction of the lam occurs only in a few nouns, such as ghayah and ayah. In the verb there is only one line which al-Farra' recited, the words of the poet:

"Fa-ka-annaha bayna al-nisa'i sabikatun ... tamshi bi-sudhdhati baytiha fa-tu'iyyu"
[Sudhdhah: the courtyard.]

"Bi-qadirin": Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: the "ba'" is extra, for emphasis, like the "ba'" in His saying: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾ [An-Nisa: 166], and His saying: ﴿A tree that grows with oil﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 20]. Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the "ba'" here is in place of the interrogative and the negation at the beginning of the speech. Al-Zajjaj said: the Arabs introduce it with negation; they say: "Ma zanantu anna Zaydan bi-qa'imin" (I did not think that Zayd was standing), and they do not say: "Zanantu anna Zaydan bi-qa'imin." It is because of the entry of "ma" and the entry of "anna" for emphasis. The implied meaning is: "Is not Allah able?" as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 81]. Ibn Mas'ud, al-A'raj, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ya'qub read "yaqdiru" (without ba'), and Abu Hatim preferred it, because the entry of the "ba'" into the predicate of "anna" is ugly. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the reading of the common people, because in the reading of 'Abd Allah it is "khalaqa al-samawati wa-al-ardha qadirun" without a ba'. And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire﴾. That is, remind them of the day when they will be exposed, and it will be said to them: "Is this not the truth?" They will say: "Yes, by our Lord!" Then the one who will rebuke them will say to them: "So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve," that is, because of your disbelief.

He said, Most High: ﴿So be patient, as the steadfast messengers were patient﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "They are those of resolve and patience." Mujahid said: "They are five: Nuh (Noah), Ibrahim (Abraham), Musa (Moses), 'Isa (Jesus), and Muhammad, peace be upon them all. They are the possessors of revealed laws (ashab al-shara'i')." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "The steadfast ones (Ulu al-'Azm) are Nuh, Hud, and Ibrahim. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to be the fourth of them." Al-Suddi said: "They are six [[What is between the two brackets is missing from manuscripts B, L and N.]]: Ibrahim, Musa, Dawud (David), Sulayman (Solomon), 'Isa, and Muhammad, may the blessings of Allah be upon them all." It was also said: "Nuh, Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Lut, and Musa, who are mentioned in sequence in the surahs al-A'raf and al-Shu'ara'." Muqatil said: "They are six: Nuh, who endured the harm of his people for a long period; Ibrahim, who endured the fire; Ishaq (Isaac), who endured being sacrificed; Ya'qub (Jacob), who endured the loss of his son and the loss of his sight; Yusuf (Joseph), who endured the well and the prison; and Ayyub (Job), who endured affliction." Ibn Jurayj said: "Among them are Isma'il, Ya'qub, and Ayyub, and among them are not Yunus, Sulayman, or Adam." Al-Sha'bi, al-Kalbi, and Mujahid also said: "They are those who were commanded to fight, who openly displayed their call and struggled against the disbelievers." It was also said: "They are the chosen messengers mentioned in the surah al-An'am [[See vol. 7, p. 35.]], and they are eighteen: Ibrahim, Ishaq, Ya'qub, Nuh, Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yusuf, Musa, Harun (Aaron), Zakariyya (Zechariah), Yahya (John), 'Isa, Ilyas (Elijah), Isma'il, al-Yasa' (Elisha), Yunus (Jonah), and Lut (Lot)." Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl preferred this view, citing His saying after it: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [[Verse 90, surah al-An'am.]] [al-An'am: 90]. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "All the messengers were possessors of resolve." This was chosen by 'Ali ibn Mahdi al-Tabari, who said: "The word 'min' (from/among) here is for specifying the kind (lil-tajnis), not for partitioning (lil-tab'id), as you would say: 'I bought robes of cloth (min al-bazz) and garments of silk (min al-khazz).' That is, be patient as the messengers were patient." It was also said: "All the prophets were possessors of resolve except Yunus ibn Matta. Do you not see that the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade that one be like him, because of the haste and impetuousness that appeared in him when he departed in anger from his people? So Allah tested him with three things: He set the 'Amaliqah (Amalekites) upon him until they raided his family and property; He set a wolf upon his son, and it devoured him; and He set a fish upon him, and it swallowed him." This was stated by Abu al-Qasim al-Hakim. Some scholars said: "The steadfast ones are twelve prophets who were sent to the Children of Israel in al-Sham (Syria), but they disobeyed them. So Allah revealed to the prophets: 'I am sending My punishment upon the disobedient Children of Israel.' This was hard for the messengers, so Allah revealed to them: 'Choose for yourselves: if you wish, I will send down punishment upon you and save the Children of Israel; and if you wish, I will save you and send the punishment upon the Children of Israel.' They consulted among themselves, and their opinion agreed that the punishment should fall upon them, and that Allah should save the Children of Israel. So Allah saved the Children of Israel and sent the punishment upon those others. He set over them the kings of the earth; some of them were sawn with saws, some had the skin of their heads and faces peeled off, some were crucified on wood until they died, and some were burned with fire." And Allah knows best. Al-Hasan said: "The steadfast ones are four: Ibrahim, Musa, Dawud, and 'Isa. As for Ibrahim, it was said to him: ﴿Submit﴾, and he said: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [[Verse 131, surah al-Baqarah.]] [al-Baqarah: 131]. Then he was tested in his wealth, his child, his homeland, and himself, and he was found truthful and faithful in all that he was tested with. As for Musa, his resolve was when his people said to him: ﴿Indeed, we are overtaken.﴾ He said: ﴿No! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾ [[Verse 61, surah al-Shu'ara'.]] [al-Shu'ara': 61–62]. As for Dawud, he committed his error, and was alerted to it, so he remained weeping for forty years until a tree grew from his tears, and he sat beneath its shade. As for 'Isa, his resolve was that he never laid one brick upon another, and he said: 'It is a passage, so cross it, and do not build upon it.'" It is as if Allah, Most High, were saying to His Messenger (ﷺ): "Be patient," meaning: be truthful in what you have been tested with, like the truthfulness of Ibrahim; be confident in the support of your Lord, like the confidence of Musa; be concerned with the lapses that have passed from you, like the concern of Dawud; and be ascetic regarding this world, like the asceticism of 'Isa. Then it was said: "This verse is abrogated (mansukhah) by the verse of the sword." And it was said: "It is muhkamah (not abrogated)." The more apparent view is that it is abrogated, because the surah is Meccan. Muqatil mentioned that this verse was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded him to be patient over what befell him, just as the steadfast messengers were patient, to make it easy for him and to strengthen him. And Allah knows best. ﴿And do not seek to hasten [the punishment]﴾. Muqatil said: "By invoking (the punishment) against them." It was also said: "In hastening the descent of punishment upon them, for their ultimate end is on the Day of Resurrection." The object of "yasta'jil" (seek to hasten) is omitted, and it is "al-'adhab" (the punishment). ﴿As if, on the day they see what they are promised﴾. Yahya said: "[That is] of the punishment." Al-Naqqash said: "Of the Hereafter." ﴿They will not have remained﴾, meaning: in the world until the punishment came upon them. This is what follows from the statement of Yahya. Al-Naqqash said: "In their graves until they were raised for the reckoning." ﴿Except an hour of a day﴾, meaning: in comparison to the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: "The terror of what they witnessed of the punishment made them forget the length of their stay in the world." Then He said: ﴿A notification﴾, meaning: this Qur'an is a notification (balagh), as al-Hasan said. "Balagh" is in the nominative case by assuming an implied subject (mubtada'), the evidence for which is His saying: ﴿This is a notification for mankind, so that they may be warned by it﴾ [[End of surah Ibrahim.]] [Ibrahim: 52], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, in this is a notification for a people who worship﴾ [[Verse 106, surah al-Anbiya'.]] [al-Anbiya': 106]. And "al-balagh" here means "al-tabligh" (conveyance). It was also said: "That is, that stay is a notification (balagh)," as Ibn 'Isa said; in this case, one pauses at "balaghin" and at "nahar." Abu Hatim mentioned that some readers paused at "wa la tasta'jil" and then began with "lahum" (for them), in the sense of "for them is a notification." Ibn al-Anbari said: "This is an error, because you have separated the 'balagh' from the lam, which is governing, by something that is not part of either of them." In Arabic it is also permissible to read "balaghan" and "balaghun": the accusative (nasb) in the sense of "except an hour, as a notification," either as a verbal noun (masdar) or as an adjective (na't) for "sa'ah" (hour); and the genitive (khafd) in the sense of "from a day is a notification." The accusative reading was recited by 'Isa ibn 'Umar and al-Hasan. It was reported from some reciters that they read "balligh" in the imperative, and on this reading the pause would be at "min nahar," then one begins with "balaghun." ﴿So will anyone be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people?﴾, meaning: those who go outside the command of Allah, as Ibn 'Abbas and others said. Ibn Muhaysin recited "fa-hal yuhlaku illa al-qawmu" (so will the people be destroyed), attributing the verb to "the people." Ibn 'Abbas said: "If a woman has difficulty in giving birth, she should write these two verses and the two words on a sheet, then wash it off and drink from it. The text is: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. There is no deity except Allah, the Great, the Forbearing, the Generous. Glory be to Allah, Lord of the heavens, Lord of the earth, and Lord of the Mighty Throne.' ﴿As if, on the day they see it, they had not remained except an evening or its morning﴾ [[End of surah al-Nazi'at.]] [al-Nazi'at: 46]. ﴿As if, on the day they see what they are promised, they had not remained except an hour of a day. A notification. So will anyone be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people?﴾ The Great Allah has spoken truly." And from Qatada: "Allah does not destroy anyone except the one who is destroyed, the polytheist [[In Tafsir al-Tabari: 'Know that none is destroyed before Allah except one who turns his back on Islam, or a hypocrite who is truthful with his tongue but contradicts with his actions.']]." It was also said: "This is the strongest verse concerning hope (al-raja')." And Allah knows best.
